title: Effect Internals: What the Elites Hide
subtitle: The insider mental model behind Effect.ts — from ZIO lineage to the data-type foundation.
throughline: One value's journey: a raw value lifted into Effect, run, wired through memoized layers and batch-preserving resolvers, and finally compared by structural equality.

chapters.title: The Mental Model and Runtime Myths
chapters.blurb: Effect is a smart, lazy, interruptible Promise — and the FUD about generators, speed, and bundle size is wrong.

steps.title: The Mental Model and Runtime Myths
steps.coverSubtitle: Effect is TypeScript's ZIO: a smart, lazy, interruptible Promise.
steps.spoken: Effect gets a bad reputation it doesn't deserve, so let's build the real mental model and dismantle the myths.
steps.displayNarration: **Effect** is TypeScript's ZIO — the same three-channel value `Effect<A, E, R>` with structured concurrency and scheduling. The fear and doubt about it gets the internals wrong.

steps.title: A value becomes a blueprint
steps.spoken: It starts with a plain value. You hand it to Effect succeed, and instead of running anything, you get back a description of a program.
steps.displayNarration: A plain value is lifted by `Effect.succeed(1)` into an `Effect<A, E, R>`. This is the core insight from the ZIO lineage: an effect is a *lazy description*, not an execution.

steps.title: Three channels, like ZIO
steps.spoken: That description carries three channels: the success type, the error type, and the requirements it needs. Effect is ZIO ported to TypeScript, with the very same shape.
steps.displayNarration: `Effect<A, E, R>` mirrors `ZIO[R, E, A]` — success, error, and requirements tracked in the types. Effect makes the environment a *union* of services where ZIO used an intersection.

steps.title: Myth: generators are slow
steps.spoken: Now the first myth. People say Effect leans on generators and generators are slow. But generators are only the API surface that mimics async await. The internals are not generator based.
steps.displayNarration: **Myth:** *Effect heavily relies on generators and generators are slow.* Reality: `Effect.gen` is only the ergonomic surface mimicking async-await — Effect's internals are **not** built on generators.

steps.title: Myth: 500x slower
steps.spoken: The second myth is that Effect is five hundred times slower. That only holds when you wrap a single addition that the compiler would turn into one CPU instruction. You would never wrap trivial arithmetic. Effect coordinates your thunks of real work.
steps.displayNarration: **Myth:** *Effect makes code 500x slower.* That figure only appears comparing `1 + 1` to `Effect.runSync(Effect.zipWith(...))` — a JIT-optimized instruction versus a coordinated program. You never wrap trivial CPU ops.

steps.title: Myth: huge bundle
steps.spoken: The third myth is bundle size. The runtime is about twenty five kilobytes gzipped, and from there Effect is fully tree shakeable, so you only pay for what you import.
steps.displayNarration: **Myth:** *The bundle size is HUGE.* Effect's runtime is ~25kb gzipped and **tree-shakeable** — you only include what you use, and terser app code often amortizes the cost.

steps.title: Micro for libraries
steps.spoken: If you write a library and even that is too much, there's Micro: a roughly five kilobyte standalone runtime with the same value shape. It drops Layer, Ref, Queue, and Deferred, but pull in any major module and the savings vanish.
steps.displayNarration: **Micro** is a ~5kb standalone runtime with `Micro<A, E, R>`, `Micro.gen`, and `MicroExit` — it omits Layer, Ref, Queue, and Deferred. Pulling in major modules negates the savings.

steps.title: Run at the edge
steps.spoken: Nothing has happened yet. Only at the edge, when you call run, does the runtime interpret the description into real work and hand back a result. Build a program as a value, and you get telemetry, dependency injection, and interruption for free.
steps.displayNarration: Only `Effect.runSync` at the edge hands the description to the **Effect Runtime**, which interprets it. The payoff of building programs as values: free telemetry, DI, and interruption.

chapters.title: Effect vs the Field
chapters.blurb: How Effect compares to Promise, neverthrow and fp-ts, and the Promise combinators — functions, not methods.

steps.title: Effect vs the Field
steps.coverSubtitle: Functions not methods, typed errors, and structured-concurrency Promise combinators.
steps.spoken: Let's place Effect next to the alternatives: plain Promises, neverthrow, fp-ts, and the Promise combinators you already know.
steps.displayNarration: Effect exposes **standalone functions** on `Either` and `Option` for `pipe` composition, where neverthrow and fp-ts use instance methods. Same ideas, better tree-shaking.

steps.title: ok becomes right
steps.spoken: Start with neverthrow. A success there is ok, a failure is err. In Effect those map directly onto Either: ok becomes right, err becomes left.
steps.displayNarration: neverthrow's `ok(...)` maps to `Either.right(...)`, and `err(...)` to `Either.left(...)`. The direct correspondence: `ok → right`, `err → left`.

steps.title: Methods versus functions
steps.spoken: The real difference is shape. neverthrow calls a method on the result. Effect calls a function on Either, like is right or map left, so you compose with pipe and the bundler drops what you don't use.
steps.displayNarration: neverthrow uses instance methods like `result.isOk()`; Effect uses functions: `Either.isRight(result)`, `Either.mapLeft(...)`. The mapping is `isOk → isRight`, `mapErr → mapLeft`.

steps.title: From Either to Effect
steps.spoken: A synchronous Either covers typed results and nothing more. Effect is the superset: it adds asynchrony, dependency injection, and interruption on top of the same typed success and error.
steps.displayNarration: A synchronous `Either` covers typed results; **Effect** adds async, dependency injection, and interruption. `Effect.either` even flips an effect's failure into an `Either` in the success channel.

steps.title: Smarter than a Promise
steps.spoken: Against a Promise, Effect wins on type safety and laziness. A Promise is eager, one shot, and untyped on errors. Effect is lazy, repeatable, and tracks errors and dependencies in the type.
steps.displayNarration: `Promise<A>` is eager, one-shot, and untyped on failure; `Effect<A, Error, Context>` is lazy, multi-shot, and statically tracks errors and dependencies.

steps.title: Promise combinators, typed
steps.spoken: Every Promise combinator has a structured concurrency twin. All matches Promise dot all, but with typed errors and automatic interruption of the losers. Combine all with either or exit and you get the behavior of all settled.
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.all({ concurrency })` is `Promise.all` with typed errors and auto-interruption. `Effect.forEach` plus `Effect.either`/`Effect.exit` mirrors `allSettled`; `Effect.raceAll` mirrors `race`/`any`.

steps.title: An un-awaited Promise
steps.spoken: And forking is the missing piece. Fork starts an effect in the background and hands you a fiber, then Fiber join reads its result later. That is exactly an un awaited Promise, but typed and interruptible.
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.fork` plus `Fiber.join` is an *un-awaited Promise* — start work in the background, read its result later, with typed errors and structured interruption.

steps.title: The whole comparison
steps.spoken: So the full picture: ok and err become right and left, methods become functions you pipe, Either grows into Effect, and every Promise combinator gains typed errors and interruption. Effect is the strict superset.
steps.displayNarration: From `Result` to `Either` to `Effect`, with `Promise` folded in: functions over methods, `Either.map`, `all`/`forEach`/`raceAll`, and `fork`+`Fiber.join`. Effect is the typed, interruptible superset.

chapters.title: Layer Memoization and Wiring
chapters.blurb: How the dependency graph is built exactly once by reference equality — and how to force or scope a rebuild.

steps.title: Layer Memoization and Wiring
steps.coverSubtitle: The dependency graph is built exactly once, by reference equality.
steps.spoken: Here's a secret the elites lean on every day: how Effect builds your dependency graph exactly once.
steps.displayNarration: Globally provided **Layers** are memoized by *reference equality* — a shared dependency is constructed a single time, no matter how many layers need it.

steps.title: A shared dependency
steps.spoken: Picture three services, A, B, and C. Both B and C depend on A. A is the value we'll follow as it flows into the graph.
steps.displayNarration: Three services where `BLive` and `CLive` both depend on `ALive`. Each is built with `Layer.effect`, and `ALive` is the shared dependency.

steps.title: Merge the graph
steps.spoken: You wire them together by providing A into both B and C and merging the result. The naive fear is that A gets built twice, once for each branch.
steps.displayNarration: `Layer.merge(Layer.provide(BLive, ALive), Layer.provide(CLive, ALive))` wires the graph. The worry: is `ALive` constructed twice, once per branch?

steps.title: Built only once
steps.spoken: It isn't. When you provide globally, layers are shared by default. A is allocated a single time and that one instance is handed to both B and C. The log prints initialized exactly once.
steps.displayNarration: Layers are **shared by default** when provided globally. `ALive` is allocated *once* and shared with both `BLive` and `CLive` — the `initialized` log fires a single time.

steps.title: By reference equality
steps.spoken: The catch is that memoization keys on reference equality. If you build a layer by calling a factory, call it once and reuse the instance. Call the factory twice and you get two different layers that won't share.
steps.displayNarration: Memoization uses **reference equality**. A layer from a factory `f()` must be created *once* and reused — calling `f` twice yields two instances that won't be shared.

steps.title: Forcing a fresh copy
steps.spoken: Sometimes you actually want a separate instance. Layer fresh forces a non shared rebuild, and Layer memoize gives you manual scoped memoization for local provides, which otherwise aren't memoized at all.
steps.displayNarration: `Layer.fresh(ALive)` forces a *non-shared* rebuild; `Layer.memoize` gives manual scoped memoization for local provides, which otherwise don't memoize.

steps.title: Effect.Service generates it
steps.spoken: To avoid the factory trap entirely, Effect Service builds the whole thing for you in one step: a Tag plus a Default layer with dependencies included, and a variant without dependencies so tests can supply their own.
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.Service<Self>()("id", {...})` generates a Tag plus `Default` (dependencies included) and `DefaultWithoutDependencies` (deps external for tests) in one step.

steps.title: Launch the graph once
steps.spoken: Put it together: A flows into B and C, they merge into one graph, shared dependencies are memoized by reference, and Layer launch runs the whole thing with every service built exactly once.
steps.displayNarration: The full wiring: `ALive` feeds `BLive` and `CLive`, `Layer.merge` composes them, and `Layer.launch` runs the graph with shared layers built exactly once. `provideMerge` would keep the provided service in the output.

chapters.title: Resolvers, Context, and Batching
chapters.blurb: Wiring service-dependent resolvers without breaking batching — the seam where DI meets request batching.

steps.title: Resolvers, Context, and Batching
steps.coverSubtitle: Wire service-dependent resolvers without one defeating the other.
steps.spoken: Now the seam where dependency injection meets batching, and where a careless resolver quietly breaks both.
steps.displayNarration: A resolver passed to `Effect.request` must have its context reduced to `never` to stay batchable. This is where **DI** and **batching** meet.

steps.title: A request is a value
steps.spoken: A request in Effect is a structured, comparable value, made with Request tagged. Because identical requests compare equal, the system can dedupe them automatically.
steps.displayNarration: A `Request.Request<Value, Error>` built with `Request.tagged("GetTodos")` is a structured, comparable value — identical requests dedupe.

steps.title: A resolver executes it
steps.spoken: Effect request ties the request to a resolver. The resolver is what actually executes it, one at a time with from effect, or in batches over an array with make batched.
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.request` ties a request to a `RequestResolver`. `RequestResolver.fromEffect` runs one at a time; `makeBatched` handles an array, completed via `Request.completeEffect`.

steps.title: The resolver needs a service
steps.spoken: Real resolvers need shared services. This one reaches for an HTTP service through a context tag and uses it to make the actual call. But pulling a service in adds it to the resolver's requirements.
steps.displayNarration: The resolver uses `Effect.andThen(HttpService, ...)` to access an `HttpService` (a `Context.Tag`) for the real fetch. But that adds `HttpService` to the resolver's `R`.

steps.title: Context can break batching
steps.spoken: Here's the trap. The context for a resolver used by Effect request is forced to never. Provide too much context, or different services to different resolvers, and they stop being compatible, so batching silently breaks.
steps.displayNarration: The context for a resolver in `Effect.request` is explicitly `never`. Varying services across resolvers makes them *incompatible for batching* — the trap.

steps.title: contextFromServices
steps.spoken: The fix is context from services. You list the exact tags the resolver touches, and it lifts your context using resolver into an effect that requires those services and returns a resolver whose own context is reduced to never.
steps.displayNarration: `RequestResolver.contextFromServices(HttpService)` lifts the resolver into `Effect<RequestResolver<GetTodos, never>, never, HttpService>` — declaring exactly which Tags it needs while the resolver's own context becomes `never`.

steps.title: Or wire it in a Layer
steps.spoken: The idiomatic alternative is to build the resolver inside Layer effect, closing over the construction time services right there. Either way the requirements are declared explicitly and batching survives.
steps.displayNarration: Alternatively, construct the resolver inside `Layer.effect`, closing over construction-time services. Either path declares requirements explicitly and preserves batching.

steps.title: Batching preserved
steps.spoken: End to end: a comparable request flows into Effect request, the resolver needs the HTTP service, context from services reduces that context to never, and now many identical requests collapse into one batched, deduplicated query.
steps.displayNarration: The full seam: `Request` to `Effect.request` to a `RequestResolver` that needs `HttpService`, with `contextFromServices` reducing `R` to `never` so requests stay **batchable and deduplicated**.

chapters.title: The Data-Type Foundation
chapters.blurb: Structural equality and the immutable data types the whole runtime quietly rests on.

steps.title: The Data-Type Foundation
steps.coverSubtitle: Structural equality and the immutable types the runtime is built on.
steps.spoken: Finally, the bedrock: the data types and the structural equality that the whole runtime quietly stands on.
steps.displayNarration: `Data` gives plain objects **value equality** and hashing so `Equal.equals` compares structure — the foundation under HashSet keys, tagged unions, and more.

steps.title: Plain objects compare by reference
steps.spoken: Two plain objects with the same fields are not equal in JavaScript, because they compare by reference. Wrap them with Data struct and they gain shallow value equality and hashing.
steps.displayNarration: Plain objects compare by *reference*. `Data.struct({ name: "Alice", age: 30 })` adds shallow **value equality** and hashing to a plain object.

steps.title: Equal.equals by structure
steps.spoken: Now Equal equals returns true when two Data values share the same structure and content. The comparison is shallow, so nested objects must also be Data values to count.
steps.displayNarration: `Equal.equals(alice, Data.struct({ name: "Alice", age: 30 }))` is `true` — structural comparison. It is *shallow*, so nested objects must also use `Data`.

steps.title: Tagged unions
steps.spoken: The same machinery powers tagged constructors and tagged enums. Data tagged and Tagged Class carry a tag, and a tagged enum gives you generated guards and matchers, dollar is and dollar match, for its union members.
steps.displayNarration: `Data.tagged`, `Data.TaggedClass`, and `Data.TaggedEnum` build tagged unions with generated `$is` and `$match` helpers — all backed by the same value-equality machinery.

steps.title: HashSet dedupes by value
steps.spoken: This is what makes hashed collections work. A HashSet dedupes its members by value equality rather than reference, and you can build one efficiently with a mutate draft. Chunk, by contrast, is only worth it for repeated concatenation.
steps.displayNarration: `HashSet` dedupes by value-equality (with `mutate` drafts), keyed through `Equal.equals`. Note: `Chunk` is only worth its overhead for *repeated concatenation*.

steps.title: The value types
steps.spoken: On top sit the everyday value types. Duration models a non negative span. DateTime now reads the Clock service, so time itself is mockable. Redacted renders as redacted to keep secrets out of logs, and BigDecimal does exact money math.
steps.displayNarration: `Duration` models non-negative spans; `DateTime.now` reads the **Clock** service so time is mockable; `Redacted` renders `<redacted>`; `BigDecimal` does exact money math.

steps.title: Equivalence and Order
steps.spoken: And underneath the comparisons are the building blocks themselves. Equivalence is compare for equality, Order is compare for sorting, and both compose with map input and combine so you derive complex comparisons from simple ones.
steps.displayNarration: `Equivalence` (compare-by-equality) and `Order` (compare-by-sorting) are the contravariant building blocks — composed via `Equivalence.mapInput`, `Order.mapInput`, and `Order.combine`.

steps.title: The whole foundation
steps.spoken: So the foundation, end to end: a plain object becomes a Data value, Equal equals compares it by structure, that powers tagged enums and hashed sets, the value types layer on, and Equivalence and Order tie the comparisons together. This is the bedrock the entire runtime rests on.
steps.displayNarration: The complete foundation: `Data` to `Equal.equals` to `TaggedEnum`, `HashSet`, the value types, and `Equivalence`/`Order`. Structural equality is the bedrock under the whole runtime.
